title: When are dividend barriers optimal?A distributional characterization in renewal risk models

paper.title: When are dividend barriers optimal? A distributional characterization in renewal risk models
paper.abstract:
Abstract We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal
risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how
claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general
assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that
exponential claims
admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading,
positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the
class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard,
every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium–discount pair for
which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon.
These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence
between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally
optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range.
Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same
mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the
structure of dividend decisions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: The optimal dividend problem is a central problem in actuarial risk theory: how much of an insurer’s surplus should be distributed to shareholders, and how much should be retained to meet future claims? The criterion introduced by de Finetti (1957) evaluates a strategy through the expected present value of dividends paid before ruin. An immediate payment reduces the funds available to support future payments; see Avanzi (2009) ; Schmidli (2008) . Barrier strategies are among the most widely studied forms of dividend policy. Their rule is transparent: pay any surplus above a prescribed level and retain the remainder. This simplicity makes it important to understand when the rule is optimal, and how that conclusion depends on the claim-size distribution. Classical results establish barrier optimality for several important risk models. Asmussen and Taksar (1997) obtain an optimal barrier in a diffusion model with unrestricted dividends. Avram et al. (2007) study the dividend problem for spectrally negative Lévy processes and express barrier values through scale functions. Loeffen (2008) gives a sufficient condition in terms of complete monotonicity of the jump density, while Kyprianou et al. (2010) ; Loeffen and Renaud (2010) relate barrier optimality to convexity properties of the jump distribution and the associated scale function. These results provide substantial classes of models in which a barrier is optimal. They do not make the barrier form universal: the examples of Azcue and Muler (2005) and the computational study of Albrecher and Garcia Flores (2023) also show the relevance of dividend strategies with several bands. Renewal arrivals introduce a further consideration. The distribution of the next claim time depends on how long the insurer has already waited since the last claim. Albrecher et al. (2005) study dividend payments under barriers with generalized Erlang interclaim times, and Mishura and Schmidli (2012) investigate barrier strategies in the same renewal setting. Albrecher and Hartinger (2006) show by a counterexample that a constant barrier need not be optimal in a Sparre Andersen model. This leaves open an important distinction: failure of a constant level does not exclude a barrier that adjusts to the time elapsed since the last claim. A finite planning horizon also allows the barrier to vary with time; De Angelis and Ekström (2017) establish such a time-dependent barrier in a diffusion dividend problem. For general renewal models, Tian et al. (2020) establish properties of the singular-dividend value function and characterize it through a constrained viscosity formulation of the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation. Liu et al. (2020) study bounded dividend rates and obtain verification and a space–time band structure under their conditions. With exponentially distributed claims and observable phases of a phase-type waiting time, Tian and Liu (2022) study optimal phase-dependent barriers. These contributions address the value equation or optimal policies in specified settings. The question considered here is which claim-size laws guarantee a barrier across premium rates, discount rates and horizons, when the controller observes claim times and sizes but no latent phases. We answer this question for each fixed renewal law with continuous hazard and uniformly bounded expected residual waiting time. Our first main result, Theorem 2.4 , proves that, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, a globally optimal barrier exists for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon if and only if the claim-size distribution is exponential . The barrier may depend on time and claim age, meaning the time since the last claim. For exponential claims we construct this barrier, prove its continuity, and establish concavity and continuous differentiability of the value in surplus. The same distributional characterization holds for age-dependent barriers on the infinite horizon. The second result, Theorem 2.5 , identifies a stronger failure for every nonexponential law in this class. There is one fixed premium–discount pair for which no globally optimal barrier exists at any sufficiently long finite horizon , or on the infinite horizon. At the same time and claim age, all of a small initial surplus should be paid immediately, whereas full payment is strictly suboptimal at a larger surplus. These decisions cannot be implemented by a single upper barrier. They also imply that the value is not concave in surplus. Thus extending the horizon cannot restore barrier optimality at these parameters, even when the barrier is allowed to depend on both time and the observed claim history through age. The main difficulty is that optimal payments depend not only on current surplus but also on the time since the last claim and the terminal date. The associated HJB equation involves three variables— time, surplus and claim age—and an integral term linking the current state to post-claim states corresponding to different claim sizes. This dependence on several variables and the nonlocal term make the optimal payment region and its boundary difficult to determine directly. We separate payments before the next claim from decisions afterwards. For exponential claims, the memoryless property permits a comparison of the benefits of retaining different amounts of capital. We show that the resulting payment decisions fit together into one barrier and verify its optimality. For nonexponential claims, we choose premium income close to the expected claim outgo and compare the consequences of paying now or retaining capital. At small reserves, delaying payment creates a loss that an optimal strategy cannot sustain; at a larger reserve, a short delay yields a strictly higher value. These comparisons prove the failure of a barrier without solving for the full optimal strategy or assuming that the value is differentiable. Our numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims while keeping the mean claim size, the claim-arrival mechanism and the economic parameters fixed. For exponential claims, the computed payment decisions have a single-barrier structure. For Gamma claims, full payment at small surplus coexists with capital retention at a larger surplus, at the same time and claim age. These decisions cannot be implemented by one upper barrier. This comparison is consistent with the theoretical analysis and shows how differences in the shape of the claim-size distribution can change dividend decisions even when the mean claim size is unchanged. Section 2 introduces the risk model and states the two main results. Section 3 establishes dynamic programming and basic value bounds. Section 4 constructs the optimal barrier for exponential claims, and Section 5 proves its failure for nonexponential claims at suitable fixed parameters. Section 6 discusses claim distributions and numerical examples. Auxiliary estimates are collected in the appendices; further examples and numerical details appear in Appendices C – F .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: The claim-size distribution can determine whether a simple dividend barrier is sufficient for optimal capital distribution. For a fixed renewal law satisfying the stated assumptions, exponential claims are exactly the distributions within the continuous IFR class that admit an optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, discount rate and finite horizon. Every nonexponential law in this class instead admits one fixed premium–discount pair at which barrier optimality fails for all sufficiently long horizons. The same distinction holds on the infinite horizon. The failure is explained by opposing initial decisions at the same time and claim age: full payment at small surplus and a strict benefit from retention at a larger surplus. The numerical comparison shows this pattern for Gamma claims at moderate parameter values, while exponential claims with the same mean give the expected barrier form. This identifies a structural consequence of choosing a claim-size law that cannot be seen from its mean alone. The bounded residual waiting-time assumption implies the existence of a positive exponential moment and excludes heavy-tailed arrivals without such moments. Extending the characterization to heavier-tailed renewal arrivals, determining the complete optimal strategy when a barrier fails, and adding explicit solvency constraints are natural further questions. Quantitative error bounds for the numerical scheme would also strengthen the comparison of dividend rules at fixed parameters.

A distributional characterization in renewal risk models Linyu Miao † † thanks: Corresponding author. Email: mly202210@126.com . Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Nankai University Affiliation: Tianjin, 300071, China October 30, 2026 Abstract We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium–discount pair for which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon. These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range. Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the structure of dividend decisions. Keywords: optimal dividends; barrier strategy; Sparre Andersen model; claim-size distribution; finite horizon; stochastic control 1 Introduction The optimal dividend problem is a central problem in actuarial risk theory: how much of an insurer’s surplus should be distributed to shareholders, and how much should be retained to meet future claims? The criterion introduced by de Finetti (1957) evaluates a strategy through the expected present value of dividends paid before ruin. An immediate payment reduces the funds available to support future payments; see Avanzi (2009) ; Schmidli (2008) . Barrier strategies are among the most widely studied forms of dividend policy. Their rule is transparent: pay any surplus above a prescribed level and retain the remainder. This simplicity makes it important to understand when the rule is optimal, and how that conclusion depends on the claim-size distribution. Classical results establish barrier optimality for several important risk models. Asmussen and Taksar (1997) obtain an optimal barrier in a diffusion model with unrestricted dividends. Avram et al. (2007) study the dividend problem for spectrally negative Lévy processes and express barrier values through scale functions. Loeffen (2008) gives a sufficient condition in terms of complete monotonicity of the jump density, while Kyprianou et al. (2010) ; Loeffen and Renaud (2010) relate barrier optimality to convexity properties of the jump distribution and the associated scale function. These results provide substantial classes of models in which a barrier is optimal. They do not make the barrier form universal: the examples of Azcue and Muler (2005) and the computational study of Albrecher and Garcia Flores (2023) also show the relevance of dividend strategies with several bands. Renewal arrivals introduce a further consideration. The distribution of the next claim time depends on how long the insurer has already waited since the last claim. Albrecher et al. (2005) study dividend payments under barriers with generalized Erlang interclaim times, and Mishura and Schmidli (2012) investigate barrier strategies in the same renewal setting. Albrecher and Hartinger (2006) show by a counterexample that a constant barrier need not be optimal in a Sparre Andersen model. This leaves open an important distinction: failure of a constant level does not exclude a barrier that adjusts to the time elapsed since the last claim. A finite planning horizon also allows the barrier to vary with time; De Angelis and Ekström (2017) establish such a time-dependent barrier in a diffusion dividend problem. For general renewal models, Tian et al. (2020) establish properties of the singular-dividend value function and characterize it through a constrained viscosity formulation of the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation. Liu et al. (2020) study bounded dividend rates and obtain verification and a space–time band structure under their conditions. With exponentially distributed claims and observable phases of a phase-type waiting time, Tian and Liu (2022) study optimal phase-dependent barriers. These contributions address the value equation or optimal policies in specified settings. The question considered here is which claim-size laws guarantee a barrier across premium rates, discount rates and horizons, when the controller observes claim times and sizes but no latent phases. We answer this question for each fixed renewal law with continuous hazard and uniformly bounded expected residual waiting time. Our first main result, Theorem 2.4 , proves that, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, a globally optimal barrier exists for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon if and only if the claim-size distribution is exponential . The barrier may depend on time and claim age, meaning the time since the last claim. For exponential claims we construct this barrier, prove its continuity, and establish concavity and continuous differentiability of the value in surplus. The same distributional characterization holds for age-dependent barriers on the infinite horizon. The second result, Theorem 2.5 , identifies a stronger failure for every nonexponential law in this class. There is one fixed premium–discount pair for which no globally optimal barrier exists at any sufficiently long finite horizon , or on the infinite horizon. At the same time and claim age, all of a small initial surplus should be paid immediately, whereas full payment is strictly suboptimal at a larger surplus. These decisions cannot be implemented by a single upper barrier. They also imply that the value is not concave in surplus. Thus extending the horizon cannot restore barrier optimality at these parameters, even when the barrier is allowed to depend on both time and the observed claim history through age. The main difficulty is that optimal payments depend not only on current surplus but also on the time since the last claim and the terminal date. The associated HJB equation involves three variables— time, surplus and claim age—and an integral term linking the current state to post-claim states corresponding to different claim sizes. This dependence on several variables and the nonlocal term make the optimal payment region and its boundary difficult to determine directly. We separate payments before the next claim from decisions afterwards. For exponential claims, the memoryless property permits a comparison of the benefits of retaining different amounts of capital. We show that the resulting payment decisions fit together into one barrier and verify its optimality. For nonexponential claims, we choose premium income close to the expected claim outgo and compare the consequences of paying now or retaining capital. At small reserves, delaying payment creates a loss that an optimal strategy cannot sustain; at a larger reserve, a short delay yields a strictly higher value. These comparisons prove the failure of a barrier without solving for the full optimal strategy or assuming that the value is differentiable. Our numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims while keeping the mean claim size, the claim-arrival mechanism and the economic parameters fixed. For exponential claims, the computed payment decisions have a single-barrier structure. For Gamma claims, full payment at small surplus coexists with capital retention at a larger surplus, at the same time and claim age. These decisions cannot be implemented by one upper barrier. This comparison is consistent with the theoretical analysis and shows how differences in the shape of the claim-size distribution can change dividend decisions even when the mean claim size is unchanged. Section 2 introduces the risk model and states the two main results. Section 3 establishes dynamic programming and basic value bounds. Section 4 constructs the optimal barrier for exponential claims, and Section 5 proves its failure for nonexponential claims at suitable fixed parameters. Section 6 discusses claim distributions and numerical examples.
